segments.t: Seeking wisdom without revealing his own predicament, Chef Barinov speaks privately with Lyova's mother, Vera Ivanovna. He claims that an unnamed friend of his got a barely known young woman pregnant, but Vera Ivanovna jumps to a very different conclusion. Let's listen to their misunderstanding in Russian.
Вера Ивановна, можно с вами поговорить?
У одного моего друга большие проблемы.
Скажите, у какого именно друга?
А вы его совсем не знаете.
Короче говоря, есть одна девушка.
Причём девушка почти совсем незнакомая.
Она беременна, а он отец.
Значит, Лёва нашёл себе девушку!
Как я рада за вашего друга!
Дети — это же просто прекрасно!
Да, но что ему теперь делать?
Ваш друг вырос настоящим мужчиной.
Он сумеет ответить за свои поступки.
Now let's trace the story that Chef Barinov tells Vera Ivanovna line by line.
Вера Ивановна, можно с вами поговорить?
'Vera Ivanovna, may I speak with you?' Barinov approaches Lyova's mother respectfully using a modal word of permission and an instrumental pronoun.
У одного моего друга большие проблемы.
'A certain friend of mine has big problems.' He disguises his own dilemma using a genitive possession phrase meaning a friend of mine.
Скажите, у какого именно друга?
'Tell me, which friend exactly?' Vera Ivanovna asks for the friend's identity in the genitive case.
А вы его совсем не знаете.
'Oh, you do not know him at all.' Barinov quickly deflects her curiosity with a negated present verb and accusative pronoun.
Короче говоря, есть одна девушка.
'In short, there is a certain young woman.' An idiomatic adverbial discourse marker means 'in short' or 'long story short'.
Причём девушка почти совсем незнакомая.
'And moreover, the girl is almost a stranger.' A connective conjunction adds an important clarifying detail to his story.
Она беременна, а он отец.
'She is pregnant, and he is the father.' He summarizes the crisis with two short present-tense predicate clauses.
Значит, Лёва нашёл себе девушку!
'So Lyova found himself a girlfriend!' Vera Ivanovna whispers to herself, assuming the anonymous friend is her shy son Lyova.
Как я рада за вашего друга!
'How happy I am for your friend!' A short feminine adjective meaning glad takes a preposition plus the accusative case for the person celebrated.
Дети — это же просто прекрасно!
'Children are simply wonderful!' She praises parenthood enthusiastically using a neuter predicate adverb meaning wonderful.
Да, но что ему теперь делать?
'Yes, but what should he do now?' Barinov presses for practical advice with a dative singular masculine pronoun.
Ваш друг вырос настоящим мужчиной.
'Your friend grew up to be a real man.' The past verb meaning grew up takes the instrumental case to describe the kind of man he became.
Он сумеет ответить за свои поступки.

'He will manage to take responsibility for his actions.' She expresses confidence in his character using a perfective future verb and an accusative prepositional phrase. Let's hear their conversation again from beginning to end.

Vera Ivanovna beams with joy at the thought of becoming a grandmother and praises her son for being a real man. Notice the instrumental noun phrase after the past verb meaning grew up. See you in the next scene.
